<reason>Side B (PRO) wins narrowly. B's deepest argument—that income and consumption taxes structurally cannot reach stock-of-wealth, while a recurring levy hits a base that persists on the balance sheet—survived the exchange, and B's reframes ("wealth-preservation system," "friction vs. invisibility," "tax the thing that stays") made the stakes memorable. B also answered pressure questions honestly, especially clarifying that the objection to death-time collection was taxpayer-controlled timing, not delay. Side A (CON) was the more disciplined technician: every rebuttal directly engaged, and A landed real hits—the two-investor return-blindness example forced B into a "rough justice" concession, and A correctly noted that annual assessment does not make statutory exemptions expire annually, undercutting B's "re-litigated every budget cycle" defense. However, A's alternative (tax gains at death) ultimately rested on "neither side can guarantee political success," an even standoff that blunted rather than won the durability clash. B's clipped opening is a small execution cost, and B4.4 sidestepped genuine-loss cases. Net: B's comparative framing plus the unrebuted structural point edge out A's tighter execution.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The A2/B4 exchange on deferral and death-time collection: A pressed that interest-bearing deferral legitimizes delayed collection, undercutting B's anti-death argument; B's reply that "buy, borrow, die" exploits death as the one valuation event taxpayers can postpone indefinitely was the sharpest single clarification of the debate and preserved B's core distinction.</best_rebuttal>
